mcqs.question: Function A is marked suspend and calls suspend function B directly, with no separate coroutine launched. Does this make A and B run concurrently?
options: No — calling one suspend function from another just chains pausing and resuming sequentially; actual concurrency requires launching separate coroutines
Yes — every suspend function call automatically runs on a separate thread
Yes, but only if both functions are marked suspend
It depends on which dispatcher A is running on
mcqs.explanation: suspend alone only means a function can pause and resume without blocking a thread — calling one suspend function from another is still sequential execution, just non-blocking while paused. Real concurrency requires explicitly launching separate coroutines (via launch or async), not merely marking functions suspend.

mcqs.question: A parent coroutine launches three child coroutines inside the same scope, and the parent's scope is cancelled. What happens to the children?
options: They continue running independently since children are not affected by parent cancellation
Only the parent is cancelled; children must be cancelled individually
They are all cancelled as well, recursively, because structured concurrency ties every coroutine's lifetime to the scope it was launched in
They pause but automatically resume once a new scope is created
mcqs.explanation: Structured concurrency guarantees that cancelling a scope cancels every coroutine launched inside it, including their own children, recursively — this is exactly what prevents a coroutine from silently outliving whatever logically owns it, without requiring manual cancellation bookkeeping.

mcqs.question: A coroutine performs a large in-memory sort of a big list. Which dispatcher should this run on, and why?
options: Dispatchers.Main, since sorting is fast enough not to matter
Dispatchers.IO, since sorting counts as I/O work
Dispatchers.Default, because the work is CPU-bound and Default's pool is sized to CPU core count specifically for that kind of work, unlike IO's larger pool meant for waiting-heavy operations
It doesn't matter which dispatcher is used as long as it's not the calling thread
mcqs.explanation: Default's pool is deliberately sized around CPU core count for work that's genuinely CPU-bound the whole time, like sorting — IO's larger, elastic pool is meant for work that spends most of its time waiting (network, disk), and running CPU-bound work there would oversubscribe CPU relative to what that pool was tuned for.

mcqs.question: A screen needs to display a database query's result and automatically update the UI whenever the underlying table changes. Which is the appropriate tool?
options: A suspend function called once in onCreate
A Flow, because it can emit multiple values over time as the underlying data changes, unlike a suspend function which produces exactly one value and completes
GlobalScope.launch with a manual polling loop
A plain Kotlin var updated from a background thread
mcqs.explanation: A suspend function gives exactly one value and finishes; a Flow can emit repeatedly over time, which is exactly the shape needed for data that should keep the UI updated as it changes — using a suspend function here would only capture the value at one moment, not future changes.

mcqs.question: A developer launches a network fetch using GlobalScope.launch instead of viewModelScope, reasoning it'll be safer from accidental cancellation. What's the actual risk?
options: GlobalScope coroutines run twice as slow as scoped ones

The coroutine is tied to the entire application's lifetime rather than the screen, so it keeps running even after the user navigates away, with no natural cancellation point and a risk of acting on state that no longer exists
GlobalScope requires a special permission declaration in the manifest
GlobalScope coroutines cannot make network calls at all
mcqs.explanation: GlobalScope deliberately has no lifecycle tie at all, which is exactly the leak structured concurrency exists to prevent — a coroutine launched there outlives the screen that started it with nothing to cancel it early, unlike viewModelScope or lifecycleScope which cancel automatically when their owner is genuinely done.

mcqs.question: A coroutine launched on Dispatchers.Main calls a synchronous, blocking file-read function directly, with no withContext wrapping. What happens?
options: The coroutine automatically moves the blocking call to a background thread
Nothing changes since coroutines make all code inside them non-blocking automatically
The call blocks the actual UI thread for its full duration, freezing rendering and input, since only genuine suspension points release the thread, not any code merely written inside a coroutine
The blocking call is silently skipped since Main dispatcher doesn't support blocking operations
mcqs.explanation: Coroutines make code read sequentially, but they only avoid blocking at genuine suspension points where a suspend function properly yields — a regular blocking call inside a coroutine still blocks the thread it's running on exactly as it would anywhere else, freezing the UI thread if run there without wrapping in withContext(Dispatchers.IO).
